```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(semTests)
```

## What do you want to test?

Suppose a factor model has two loadings, `a` and `b`, and we want to test
whether they are equal. We can examine the score after imposing equality, or
compare the fitting criteria with and without equality. Both are tests of a
*restriction within a model*. Testing whether the whole model fits the
population moments exactly is a separate question.

`semtest()` builds all of these tests. Its first argument is the model fitted
under the null. The second, when present, is the alternative.

| Question | Call | Fits needed |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Does the whole model fit exactly? | `semtest(fit)` | The proposed model |
| Can the equality restriction be released? | `semtest(restricted, fit)` | The restricted model and an alternative specification |
| Does equality leave the population minimum criterion unchanged? | `semtest(restricted, fit, statistic = "criterion")` | Both models |

`pvalues_nested()` also compares nested models, but it tests a different null:
that both models fit exactly, using Satorra's (2000) construction. The nested
tests in this vignette allow the larger model to be misspecified, as explained
below, so the two need not agree.

We first work through the equality restriction using complete continuous data.

## One restriction, two tests

```{r models, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.alt="Two one-factor models with four indicators. The unrestricted model has loadings a and b on x2 and x3; the restricted model uses the same loading on both paths.", fig.cap="The same factor model before and after imposing equality. Blue paths identify the restriction. Residuals are uncorrelated; intercepts and variances are omitted from the drawing."}
knitr::include_graphics(if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  "figures/restriction-models.pdf"
} else {
  "figures/restriction-models.svg"
})
```

The first loading is fixed to 1 in both models, so their factor scales agree.
The loadings of `x2` and `x3` are labeled `a` and `b`. Our null is `a = b`;
the loading of `x4`, variances, and intercepts remain free in both models.

```{r fits}
d <- lavaan::HolzingerSwineford1939
model <- "f =~ x1 + a*x2 + b*x3 + x4"
fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, d, meanstructure = TRUE)
restricted <- lavaan::cfa(paste(model, "a == b", sep = "\n"),
                          d, meanstructure = TRUE)
lavaan::coef(fit)[c("a", "b")]
```

### Score: evaluate the restricted fit

The score test starts at the restricted fit and measures how strongly the data
pull away from `a = b` once the other free parameters have adjusted. This
adjustment is called profiling.

```{r score}
score <- semtest(restricted, fit)
score
```

Only the restricted fit needs to be optimized. We reuse `fit` to supply the
alternative parameterization, but an unfitted template works as well:

```{r template}
template <- lavaan::cfa(model, d, meanstructure = TRUE, do.fit = FALSE)
semtest(restricted, template)
```

Nested models must use the same data, criterion, factor scaling, and aligned
parameterization. Keeping the same model syntax and adding an equality
constraint, as above, makes that relationship explicit.

### Criterion difference: compare both fits

This test uses the increase in the fitted criterion caused by equality. Both
models must be optimized. The reference distribution is calculated at the
restricted fit.

```{r criterion}
criterion <- semtest(restricted, fit, statistic = "criterion")
criterion
```

For this regular nested comparison, the null says the population minimum
criterion is unchanged by the restriction. Under the common-target assumptions
discussed below, that is the same equality restriction the score test
addresses. Their sample statistics and p-values need not coincide.

```{r comparison, echo=FALSE}
comparison <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Score", "Criterion difference"),
  Statistic = c(score$statistic, criterion$statistic),
  `p-value` = c(score$p_value, criterion$p_value),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 4)
```

Neither test rejects equality at the 5% level (*p* =
`r sprintf("%.3f", score$p_value)` and `r sprintf("%.3f", criterion$p_value)`). Neither
test says whether the factor model as a whole fits, and the global test below
rejects exact fit. The next section explains what a restriction test means in
that case.

## What if the factor model is misspecified?

A model can fail to reproduce the population moments even at its best-fitting
parameter value. That value is the *pseudo-parameter*: the minimizer of the
population fitting criterion. Under structural misspecification, `a = b`
refers to its two loadings, rather than to parameters of a true factor model.
The target can depend on the fitting criterion.

For nested inference, we require a shared criterion and, under the null, a
common population minimizer in the restricted model. We also need the usual
local regularity conditions, including identification and suitable curvature.
A sandwich calculation does not remove those requirements.

It helps to distinguish four issues:

* **Nonnormality:** the observations need not follow a normal distribution,
  even when the model reproduces their means and covariances.
* **Structural misspecification:** the model cannot reproduce the target
  moments; restrictions concern the criterion's pseudo-parameter.
* **Missing data:** FIML uses the observed-data likelihood contributions.
  Its population target also depends on the observation process and assumptions.
* **Estimated fitting weights:** for weighted least squares, the criterion's
  weight matrix is estimated from the same data as the sample moments.

Satorra (1989) gives a unified treatment of restriction tests, and Satorra
(2000) develops scaled and adjusted versions under nonnormality. The
extensions to missing data, structural misspecification, and estimated
fitting weights used here are developed in manuscripts in preparation.

## How the statistic and its reference are formed

Two separate decisions shape a score test: which matrix weights its quadratic
form, and how the underlying matrices are estimated. `semtest()` takes the
first as its `weight` argument. The second belongs to `inference_control()`,
whose settings can also be passed to `semtest()` directly.

Write $s$ for the score at the restricted fit, $H$ for the curvature of
the fitting criterion (how the score changes with the parameters), and $J$
for the covariance of the score. Profiling uses $H$ to remove the directions
in which the restricted model can still move. Call the profiled score
$\tilde s$, its covariance $\tilde J$, and the profiled weight matrix
$\tilde M$. The statistic is
$$
T = \tilde s^{\mathsf T} \tilde M^{-1} \tilde s .
$$
Its reference distribution is a weighted sum of independent $\chi^2_1$
variables, weighted by the eigenvalues of $\tilde M^{-1} \tilde J$.
Here curvature means $H$ itself, not its inverse.

`weight` chooses $M$:

* `"curvature"`, the default, uses $H$ itself.
* `"expected_curvature"` uses the expected curvature even when $H$ is the
  observed curvature. This keeps observed curvature in the profiling, which
  the limit requires when the model may be misspecified, while weighting by
  the more stable expected matrix.
* `"score_covariance"` uses $J$. Every eigenvalue is then 1, and $T$ has
  a chi-square reference: the score is fully studentized.

The criterion difference always weights by curvature, so `weight` does not
apply to it.

With a single restriction there is a single eigenvalue, and all three
weightings give the same p-value, although the statistics differ. The choice
matters when several restrictions are tested jointly. Here all three free
loadings are held equal:

```{r weights}
model3 <- "f =~ x1 + a*x2 + b*x3 + c*x4"
fit3 <- lavaan::cfa(model3, d, meanstructure = TRUE)
equal3 <- lavaan::cfa(paste(model3, "a == b", "b == c", sep = "\n"),
                      d, meanstructure = TRUE)
weights <- c("curvature", "expected_curvature", "score_covariance")
do.call(rbind, lapply(weights, function(w) {
  test <- semtest(equal3, fit3, weight = w)
  data.frame(weight = w, statistic = test$statistic, df = test$df,
             reference = test$reference, p_value = test$p_value)
}))
```

### Conventions: `inference_control()`

```{r control}
inference_control()
```

* `curvature` chooses observed or expected $H$. The two agree in probability
  when the model is correctly specified and can differ when it is not.
* `score_covariance` chooses how $J$ is estimated. `"centered"` subtracts
  the score means within each group and stays valid when the score does not
  have mean zero. `"uncentered"` uses raw score products, which is consistent
  only when the score has mean zero.
* `weight_effect` decides whether estimating the fitting weights counts as a
  source of sampling variability. It matters only for least squares.
* `derivative_step`, `tolerance`, and `keep` control the numerical work.

`curvature` and `score_covariance` are shown as `<by test>`: each test picks
the convention suited to its null. Overall fit assumes the model holds, since
that is its hypothesis, and uses expected curvature with uncentered score
products. Nested tests allow the larger model to be misspecified, and use
observed curvature with centered products. Supplying a value overrides the
choice. These two calls are equivalent:

```{r control-override}
semtest(equal3, fit3, curvature = "expected")
semtest(equal3, fit3, control = inference_control(curvature = "expected"))
```

With expected curvature, a nested test is valid only when the larger model is
correctly specified.

### Choosing a p-value calibration

Each test returns a `semTests_test` object holding its statistic, eigenvalues,
reference distribution, and default p-value. `pvalues()` evaluates other
calibrations from that object, without recomputing anything from the fits:

```{r calibrations}
test3 <- semtest(equal3, fit3)
test3$eigenvalues
pvalues(test3, c("ALL", "SB", "SS", "PEBA2"))
```

`ALL` evaluates the weighted chi-square distribution itself. `SB` and `SS` are
the Satorra–Bentler scaled and scaled-and-shifted approximations, and
`PEBA2` is penalized eigenvalue block averaging with two blocks. These are
calibrations of the same statistic. They do not change its curvature, score
covariance, or weight. Fully studentized tests accept only `STD`, since their
reference is already chi-square.

The penalized methods were evaluated for the statistics of `pvalues()` and
`pvalues_nested()`, not for score tests.

## Global exact fit

Return now to the separate question: does the unrestricted factor model fit
the population moments exactly?

```{r global}
global <- semtest(fit)
global
pvalues(global, c("SB", "ALL"))
```

This compares the fitted model with saturated means and covariances, using
likelihood scores at the fitted moments. Rejection concerns the whole model,
not specifically the equality of `a` and `b`. The robust reference handles
nonnormality, but the null is still exact fit.

For overall fit, `curvature` refers to the curvature of the saturated model.
The classical discrepancy statistic for the same question is what
`pvalues(fit)` computes, so `semtest()` does not duplicate it:
`statistic = "criterion"` requires an alternative.

## Missing data and estimated fitting weights

| Setting | Overall fit | Nested score and criterion |
|:--|:--:|:--:|
| Complete continuous ML | Yes | Yes |
| Continuous FIML | Yes | Yes |
| Complete continuous GLS/WLS/DWLS/ULS | No | Yes |
| Complete all-ordered DWLS/WLS/ULS | No | Yes |

`pvalues()` and `pvalues_nested()` keep their own scope; see
`?semTests-support`.

For FIML, likelihood scores are observed-data scores for each missingness
pattern, and the score covariance is their empirical covariance, as for
complete data. See `vignette("fiml-missing-data", package = "semTests")` for
the missing-data workflow. `"STD"` gives the non-robust reference, which
assumes the information equality:

```{r fiml}
d_missing <- d
set.seed(1)
d_missing$x2[sample(nrow(d), 60)] <- NA
fit_fiml <- lavaan::cfa(model, d_missing, meanstructure = TRUE,
                        missing = "fiml")
pvalues(semtest(fit_fiml), c("STD", "SB", "ALL"))
```

For least squares, the *fitting weights* are the matrix weighting discrepancies
between observed and model-implied moments. They are not sampling weights.
Their estimation can contribute to sampling variability when the structural
model is misspecified. The contribution vanishes at exact fit.

Here is the equality of all three loadings, fitted by continuous DWLS:

```{r weights-dwls}
fit_dwls <- lavaan::cfa(model3, d, meanstructure = TRUE, estimator = "DWLS",
                        ordered = FALSE)
equal_dwls <- lavaan::cfa(paste(model3, "a == b", "b == c", sep = "\n"), d,
                          meanstructure = TRUE, estimator = "DWLS",
                          ordered = FALSE)
semtest(equal_dwls, fit_dwls, weight = "score_covariance")
semtest(equal_dwls, fit_dwls, weight = "score_covariance",
        weight_effect = "fixed")
```

The default, `weight_effect = "estimated"`, includes the sampling variability
of both the sample moments and the estimated fitting weights. `"fixed"` treats
the weights as known, which is correct only when the model fits exactly.
Least-squares tests require the centered score covariance, which is the
nested default.

These tests currently exclude sampling weights, clusters, nonlinear
constraints, and parameter bounds. The ordinal path requires complete,
all-ordered data with nonempty pairwise cells; it does not support mixed
indicators or pairwise missingness. See
`vignette("categorical-data", package = "semTests")` for ordinal fitting.

## Inspecting a result

Pass `keep = TRUE` to retain the numerical ingredients in `$ingredients`, and
inspect `$diagnostics` and `$provenance` when checking a calculation. For
example, the nuisance stationarity norm checks that the restricted fit is a
stationary point of its own criterion:

```{r inspect}
score$diagnostics$nuisance_stationarity_norm
```

For ordinal data, the first-stage influence of the thresholds and polychoric
correlations is computed in closed form, using lavaan's score-product
convention for the first-stage weight. The derivative of the estimated weight
is also closed form for DWLS and ULS. Full WLS differentiates its weight
numerically, which can be slow with many distinct response patterns.

## References

Satorra, A. (1989). Alternative test criteria in covariance structure analysis:
A unified approach. *Psychometrika*, 54, 131–151.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294453>

Satorra, A. (2000). Scaled and adjusted restricted tests in multi-sample analysis
of moment structures. In R. D. H. Heijmans, D. S. G. Pollock, & A. Satorra
(Eds.), *Innovations in Multivariate Statistical Analysis* (pp. 233–247).
Kluwer Academic. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4615-4603-0_17>
